events.title: A village by the river
events.description: A few hundred people farm the fields on both banks. A watermill grinds their grain, and the church is the tallest thing for miles. Almost everyone walks; the river is the main road.
keyPoints: Most people live and work on farms
Water power runs the mill
The river carries goods to the coast

events.title: The port opens
events.description: Merchants build a stone quay and brick warehouses on the north bank. Sailing ships load grain and timber and bring back cloth, sugar and tea. The town grows around the trade.
keyPoints: Stone quays let ships tie up beside the warehouses
Trade by water was far cheaper than by road
A wooden bridge joins the two banks in 1765

events.title: A canal is dug
events.description: Investors pay for a canal so barges can bring coal straight to the river. The 1790s were the height of Britain's canal mania, when dozens of canals were approved in a few years.
keyPoints: A horse could pull about 30 tonnes on a canal barge
Cheap coal makes new industry possible
Most canal work was dug by hand

events.title: Gas lights the streets
events.description: Gas made from coal is piped under the streets to lamps along the quay. London's Pall Mall got the first gas street lights in 1807, and cities across Europe followed within twenty years.
keyPoints: Lamplighters lit each lamp by hand every evening
Streets became safer after dark
Gas came from heating coal in a gasworks

events.title: The railway arrives
events.when: 1838 · eight years after the first intercity line
events.description: A steam railway reaches the south bank, with a grand station and an iron and glass train shed. The world's first intercity passenger line, Liverpool to Manchester, opened in 1830; within twenty years railways linked most large towns.
keyPoints: A journey that took a day by coach takes an hour or two
Railway time made towns set their clocks to one standard
New streets of houses grow up around the station

events.title: Factories and smokestacks
events.description: Steam-powered mills and works fill the south-east bank, and tall chimneys carry their smoke above the rooftops. Rows of terraced houses go up fast for the workers who pour in from the countryside.
keyPoints: The town's population multiplies within a lifetime
Coal smoke blackens buildings and lungs
Long shifts, six days a week, even for children

events.title: Electric light
events.description: Electric street lamps replace the gas lamps along the quay. In 1882 Edison's Pearl Street Station in New York and the Holborn Viaduct station in London began supplying electricity to paying customers.
keyPoints: Arc lamps and then bulbs replace gas flames
Power stations send electricity through cables
Electricity soon drives trams and lifts too

events.title: A steel bridge
events.description: The old wooden bridge comes down and a steel arch bridge goes up, strong enough for heavy carts and, soon, trams. Steel had become cheap after the Bessemer process of the 1850s.
keyPoints: Steel is stronger and lighter than iron
The arch carries the deck on hangers
Painted red to keep off rust

events.title: Electric trams
events.description: Electric trams run across the bridge, fed by a wire overhead. The first electric tram line opened near Berlin in 1881, and by 1900 most big cities had them.
keyPoints: Trams let workers live further from the factories
A pole on the roof touches the overhead wire
Horse trams had run on rails before this

events.title: Skyscrapers
events.description: Steel frames and safe passenger lifts let buildings climb past ten storeys. The first steel-frame skyscraper, Chicago's Home Insurance Building, went up in 1885. Our stepped art deco tower is finished in 1931, the same year as New York's Empire State Building.
keyPoints: The steel frame carries the weight, not the walls
Otis's safety lift made tall buildings practical
Land in the centre becomes very expensive

events.title: Highways and cars
events.description: Cars fill the streets. An elevated highway is built along the north bank, cutting the old town off from its river. The trams are scrapped the same year, as they were in many cities in the 1950s.
keyPoints: The US Interstate Highway Act passed in 1956
Cities rebuilt their streets around cars
Riverside land becomes roads and car parks

events.title: Glass towers
events.description: Offices in glass and steel boxes replace old blocks. The style came from buildings like New York's Lever House (1952) and Seagram Building (1958): a frame hung with a thin curtain wall of glass.
keyPoints: Curtain walls carry no weight
Air conditioning makes sealed glass towers livable
The business district moves west

events.title: The factories close
events.description: Work moves to cheaper places and the mills shut one by one. The smoke stops. Like many industrial cities in the 1970s and 1980s, the town loses jobs and people.
keyPoints: Containers and cheap shipping move factories abroad
Old works sit empty and polluted
The steam trains have already gone; electric trains took over in the 1960s

events.title: A park on the old works
events.description: The cleaned-up works become a park with a pond, and one chimney is kept as a monument. Germany's Landscape Park Duisburg-Nord (1994) and Seattle's Gas Works Park (1975) turned old industry into parks the same way.
keyPoints: Polluted soil is capped or cleaned
Old industrial landmarks are kept as reminders
The warehouses become flats and studios

events.title: The highway comes down
events.description: The elevated highway is torn down and the waterfront becomes a tree-lined promenade again. San Francisco removed its Embarcadero Freeway in 1991, and Seoul uncovered the Cheonggyecheon stream in 2005.
keyPoints: Traffic moves to a ring road
People can walk to the river again
Land values beside the water rise

events.title: Today
events.description: Trams are back as modern light rail, the tallest tower has a garden on its roof, and boats carry visitors past the old mill. The church, the mill and one chimney still stand among glass towers three centuries younger.
keyPoints: Many cities rebuilt tram lines from the 1980s on
Old buildings get new uses
More than half of all people now live in cities

farm.name: Farm
farm.description: A farmhouse and barn. Most families in 1700 grow their own food and sell the rest at the market.

river.name: The river
river.description: The reason the town is here: fresh water, power for the mill, and a road to the sea.

descriptions.text: A cluster of cottages around the church and the market place.
Cottages give way to taller townhouses as trade brings money in.
The east side becomes the business district, with the town's first skyscrapers.
Cut off from the river by the elevated highway.
Joined to the river again by the new promenade.
A muddy riverbank where boats pull up.
Stone quays and warehouses: the busy heart of the port.
Ships have outgrown the river; the docks go quiet.
The warehouses are converted into flats and studios.
Fields beyond the edge of town.
Blocks of flats for a growing population.
Glass office towers rise as banks and offices move in.
Farmland on the south bank.
Streets of terraced houses grow up around the new railway station.
Fields and a farm.
The industrial quarter: mills, works and chimneys.
Factories closing one after another.
A park with a pond, built on the old works.
The oldest building in town and the tallest for over 150 years.
Now dwarfed by the new skyscrapers around it.
Still standing among glass towers, three centuries on.
The river turns the wheel, and the wheel turns millstones that grind grain into flour.
Steam and electric mills have taken its work. The wheel has stopped.
Restored as a café and small museum.
Brick stores for grain, timber and imported goods, right on the quay.
Standing empty as shipping moves to big container ports.
Converted into flats, studios and restaurants.
Wooden sailing ships carrying grain, timber and cloth.
A steamship: no more waiting for the wind.
A sightseeing boat for visitors.

canal.name: Canal
canal.description: Dug by hand to bring coal barges to the river. Horses walked the towpath pulling the boats.

railway.name: Railway line
railway.description: The line that brought the industrial age to town.

descriptions.text: A grand stone station and an iron and glass train shed.
Restored, with a new glass roof on the old shed.
A steam locomotive pulling passenger carriages.
An electric train: quieter, cleaner and faster.

riverside-works.name: Riverside works
riverside-works.description: The first big factory in town: a steam-powered textile mill employing hundreds of workers.

factories.name: Factory
factories.description: Steam engines drive the machines inside; coal smoke pours from the chimney.

descriptions.text: The chimney of the riverside works, 42 metres of brick.
The works have closed, but the chimney is kept as a monument in the new park.

smoke.name: Coal smoke
smoke.description: Soot and sulphur from burning coal. It blackened buildings and caused deadly smogs in industrial cities.

descriptions.text: Rows of small brick houses built quickly for factory workers, often two rooms up and two down.
Some rows are cleared for modern blocks of flats.

wooden-bridge.name: Wooden bridge
wooden-bridge.description: A timber bridge on wooden piles. Before it, people crossed by ferry.

bridge.name: Steel arch bridge
bridge.description: A through-arch bridge: the deck hangs from two red steel arches.

tram.name: Electric tram
tram.description: Powered from an overhead wire through the pole on its roof.

light-rail.name: Light rail
light-rail.description: Trams are back: modern, low-floor and electric.

gas-lamps.name: Gas lamp
gas-lamps.description: Coal gas burned in a glass lantern. A lamplighter lit it every evening.

electric-lamps.name: Electric streetlight
electric-lamps.description: Brighter than gas, and switched on from a power station.

highway.name: Elevated highway
highway.description: A raised road for cars along the river. Fast for drivers, but it walled the town off from the water.

ring-road.name: Ring road
ring-road.description: Takes through traffic around the centre instead of through it.

cars.name: Cars
cars.description: Mass-produced cars filled the streets after the Second World War.

promenade.name: Riverside promenade
promenade.description: Trees and a footpath where the elevated highway used to run.

park.name: Works Park
park.description: A pond and trees on cleaned-up factory land.

exchange.name: Exchange Building
exchange.description: The town's first skyscraper: a steel frame clad in stone, with lifts to every floor.

meridian.name: Meridian Tower
meridian.description: Stepped back as it rises, like the New York towers of the time, and topped with a spire.

glass-tower.name: Glass tower
glass-tower.description: A plain box with a glass curtain wall, the office building of its age.

river-spire.name: River Spire
river-spire.description: The tallest building in town, with a garden on its roof.
